A windowsill is the flat, horizontal ledge at the very bottom of a window. Think of it as a narrow shelf that is built right into the base of a window opening. It runs the full width of the window, left to right.

Picture a window on a wall. The window has a frame around it — a border of wood, metal, or plastic that holds the glass in place. Now look at the very bottom edge of that frame. The flat, outward-sticking surface right there — the part that is roughly at the level of the glass's lowest edge — is the windowsill.

It sits where the window meets the wall below it.

A windowsill is a flat, usually rectangular surface. It is wider than the wall is thick, so it sticks out a little — both into the room on the inside, and outward from the building on the outside. It is not a deep surface; it is more like a wide ledge than a table. Its depth (front to back) is usually just a few centimetres to about 15–25 centimetres, depending on the thickness of the wall and the design of the window.

Every window actually has two windowsills:

  • The interior windowsill — this is the one inside your room, on the inside of the wall. It faces upward into the room. This is the one people most commonly refer to in everyday speech when they say "windowsill."
  • The exterior windowsill (sometimes called the window ledge) — this is the one on the outside of the building. It faces outward and slightly downward, and is specifically shaped to allow rainwater to run off instead of soaking into the wall. This outer one is sometimes just called the "window ledge" to distinguish it from the inner one, though the two terms overlap in casual use.

In everyday conversation, when someone says "windowsill" without any extra explanation, they almost always mean the interior one — the flat ledge inside the room.

The material depends on the window and the building:

  • Wood — the most traditional and common material, especially in older homes.
  • Stone or marble — found in older, grander buildings; very durable and attractive.
  • PVC or vinyl — common in modern homes; easy to clean and resistant to moisture.
  • Concrete or brick — often seen in industrial-style buildings or on exterior sills.
  • Tile — sometimes used on interior sills in kitchens or bathrooms.

The windowsill serves both a practical and a decorative purpose.

Practically:

  • On the exterior, it channels rainwater away from the wall, protecting the building from water damage.
  • On the interior, it closes the gap between the window frame and the inner wall, giving the window a neat, finished appearance.

In everyday life, people use the interior windowsill to:

  • Place potted plants, since the sill gets natural sunlight from the window.
  • Display decorative objects like candles, small sculptures, or framed photos.
  • Rest small items temporarily — a book, a cup of tea, your phone.
  • Sit and lean against while looking outside, especially in bay windows where the sill can be wide enough to sit on.
  • In older homes, people sometimes kept perishable food cool on the outer sill before refrigerators were common.

These two terms are often used interchangeably, and in casual conversation that is perfectly fine. However, if you want to be precise:

  • Windowsill most naturally refers to the flat ledge inside the room, at the base of the window.
  • Window ledge can refer to either the inside or outside ledge, but is used especially for the exterior one — the protruding stone or concrete shelf visible from outside the building.

In practice, most people use both terms loosely and are understood without confusion.

• She placed a small cactus on the windowsill where it could get enough sunlight.
  • The cat curled up on the windowsill and watched the street below.
  • He rested his arms on the windowsill and gazed out at the rain.
  • The paint on the old wooden windowsill had started to peel and crack.
  • Pigeons often land on the exterior windowsill of their apartment.

A windowsill is the flat, shelf-like ledge built into the bottom of a window. Inside a room, it is the surface people place plants and objects on and lean against. Outside a building, it is the protruding ledge that keeps water from running down the wall. It is a simple but essential part of any window's structure and plays both a functional and a decorative role in architecture and home life.
